papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical ways to transfer performance from large, expensive models to smaller, faster ones. The literature spans soft-label distillation from ensembles, feature- and representation-based matching, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, task-adaptive compression for large pretrained language models, and methods to transfer non-standard properties such as adversarial robustness. Empirical results demonstrate that properly designed distillation procedures can retain much of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, that internal-representation matching often improves downstream generalization beyond logits-only approaches, and that KD variants can be adapted to constraints such as limited (or private) data, distributed training, and resource- or latency-aware deployment. Open challenges include understanding which aspects of teacher knowledge are most useful for which student architectures and tasks, designing distillation under strict privacy or data-availability constraints, and transferring robustness properties reliably.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Constraints, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible set of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller student models so that compact models retain much of the utility of high-capacity systems. KD operates across levels of abstraction (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational structure) and is routinely combined with complementary compression strategies (quantization, pruning, architecture search) and data strategies (use of original data, augmentation, or synthesized inputs). Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many settings, but success is context-dependent: it depends on the choice of distilled signals, teacher preparation, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of distillation data, and deployment constraints such as latency, privacy, or robustness. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, practical variants, and actionable recommendations for applying KD effectively in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Vaughn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression: Centrality, Mechanisms, and Conditional Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed as part of a broader compression pipeline—combining choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to supply or synthesize distillation data—KD can recover much of teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. However, its effectiveness is conditional: data availability, teacher–student heterogeneity, capacity limits, and risks of propagating teacher errors or biases require task-aware recipes and complementary techniques to produce reliable, production-ready compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Wise
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Task-Aware Remedies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, flexible suite of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while often retaining most task performance. Empirical work demonstrates KD’s effectiveness across modalities and tasks, but also reveals systematic limitations arising from teacher-student capacity mismatch, optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and the sample-wise effects of soft targets. To make distillation reliably useful in production and research, practitioners should pair KD with task-aware layer selection, representation-level supervision, careful sample weighting, and complementary compression methods such as pruning or quantization. This balanced approach preserves KD’s deployment advantages while mitigating its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Capabilities, Limits, and Complementary Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, production-ready strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations across many tasks and modalities, enabling substantial reductions in parameters and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not sufficient by itself in all settings: its success depends on what is distilled, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases or errors. For robust, deployable compression, KD should be treated as the central element of a broader pipeline that includes data synthesis or augmentation, architecture-aware design, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, or progressive module replacement), plus careful attention to privacy, fairness, and domain-shift risks.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single training trick into a flexible, task-aware toolkit for shrinking large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, KD methods transfer teacher signals at different levels — final soft outputs, intermediate features, relational or attention structure — and are often combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical success depends on aligning teacher and student capacity, choosing what and how to transfer, handling data availability (including data-free scenarios), and addressing robustness and privacy constraints. When KD is designed with these considerations it can substantially reduce inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance, though open problems remain around domain shift, rare-token behaviors, and reliably transferring robustness.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers the behavior of larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining task performance. The literature defines a flexible toolkit of objectives (soft logits, feature/attention matching, relational losses), training schedules (multi-stage, online, multi-teacher), and data strategies (use of original, augmented, synthetic, or data-free inputs). Empirical work shows KD combined with pretraining and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation) yields compact models that approach teacher accuracy, but practical success requires careful choices about what to transfer, student capacity, data availability, and robustness or fairness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compressing and Adapting Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Across settings—domain adaptation, resource-constrained deployment, privacy-limited releases, sequence generation, and large-scale distributed training—distillation methods enable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and cost. By leveraging teacher signals (soft targets, feature representations, or ensembles), self-distillation, and data- or communication-efficient protocols, practitioners can tailor compression strategies to meet production constraints without wholesale redesign of model architectures.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Necessary Precautions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach for turning large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students. As a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD transfers predictive behavior and internal structure via soft targets, intermediate-feature alignment, attention maps, and relational objectives. When integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with careful data and architecture design, KD routinely yields compact models that preserve much of teacher performance and enable latency-, memory-, or privacy-constrained deployment. However, KD’s benefits are contingent on student capacity, data availability and provenance, teacher artifacts, and distributional shift; addressing these requires deliberate, task-aware pipelines and evaluation tailored to real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a set of teacher→student techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving students. Across vision and NLP, KD variants include soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and feature-level imitation, relational or structure-preserving losses, multi-teacher ensembles, data-agnostic or data-free procedures, and self- or cross-supervised transfer. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing compact models but requires careful handling of data regimes, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and robustness or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. The field includes matching softened output distributions, imitating intermediate representations or attention maps, transferring relational or structural knowledge, and combining distillation with data-side techniques (augmentation, synthetic data) and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing parameters and latency, but effectiveness depends on choices of knowledge to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and task-specific constraints. Remaining challenges include robustness under domain shift, fairness and bias transfer, privacy in distributed settings, and limits to compression for some generative tasks.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression and Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick but a core engineering technique that enables deployment, adaptation, privacy, and robustness for large neural models in real-world systems. By treating distillation as a family of methods—ranging from output soft-target transfer to feature- and layer-wise alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols—practitioners can compress models while preserving task performance and satisfying latency, memory, and data-privacy constraints. Thoughtful application of KD, combined with complementary methods (pretraining, projector design, multi-stage schedules, and careful handling of teacher imperfections), yields compact models that are practical for production while exposing clear avenues for further research.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central Tool That Must Be Used as a Toolkit for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a vital method for turning large, high-performing deep models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, speech, and NLP shows that matching teacher outputs and internal signals can yield students that recover much of teacher accuracy while delivering large gains in latency, memory, and energy. However, KD is not a single recipe: practical success depends on which teacher signals are transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, what data are used (real, augmented, or synthetic), and whether distillation is combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Careful, task-aware design and hybrid pipelines are therefore required to realize robust, production-ready compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: A Task-Aware Argument
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, practical engine of model compression: when applied as an integrated, task-aware system it enables compact students that preserve much of a teacher’s utility while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware surgery), careful data strategies (augmentation, synthesis, or data-free protocols), and explicit attention to teacher–student capacity alignment and robustness evaluation. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its benefits are conditional on signal selection, data and initialization choices, and evaluation for fairness and domain-shift resilience. I argue for treating KD as a configurable pipeline (signals, data, architecture, optimization) and for adopting specific practices that mitigate common failure modes in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Juarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a multifaceted set of techniques for creating smaller, faster models from large neural teachers. Methods span soft-output transfer, intermediate-representation and attention matching, relational/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-centric strategies including synthetic or data-free approaches. KD is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows strong practical gains across NLP and other modalities, but success depends on careful alignment of teacher and student, data strategies, and attention to robustness and domain-shift limitations.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger teacher models into smaller students to reduce inference cost and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Methods range from matching softened output distributions to aligning intermediate features, attention patterns, or relational structure, and often combine distillation with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled models can recover much of teacher performance on vision and language tasks, but success depends on what is transferred, how teachers and students are matched, data availability and selection, and training protocols. Practical deployment requires addressing optimization challenges, teacher imperfection, domain shift, and distributional issues such as low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Webb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other structural signals from teacher to student. KD can yield large wins in latency, memory, and deployability when integrated with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression methods, but its success is conditional on teacher–student alignment, the choice of distilled signals, data availability (or synthesis), and explicit validation for robustness and fairness. Treating KD as a configurable pipeline rather than a single recipe produces the most reliable practical outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Stein
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Work has expanded beyond the original teacher→student soft-label matching to include intermediate-representation imitation, multi-teacher and adaptive-teacher schedules, self- and teacher-free variants, and data-aware protocols (including data-free and privacy-preserving approaches). Empirical and theoretical analyses show KD can preserve much of teacher performance while substantially lowering latency, memory, and sometimes communication cost; success depends on matching distillation signals to student capacity, handling data heterogeneity, and combining KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Remaining challenges include robustness to domain shift and adversaries, preserving rare-token or long-tail behaviors, automating signal and teacher selection, and reliable operation without original training data.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Current Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and graph domains, KD has been adapted into many variants — matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, progressive module replacement, online/multi-teacher training, and data-free or privacy-aware pipelines — often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation targets, student preparation, and data strategies are chosen carefully. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness is limited by teacher quality, data availability or privacy, teacher–student architectural mismatch, and risks of transferring undesirable teacher behaviors. Practical deployment benefits from combining KD with complementary compression and data strategies, designing student-aware teacher signals, and accounting for robustness and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Work across NLP and broader deep learning has developed multiple KD paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate-representation matching, layer-to-layer and many-to-many layer mapping, multi-teacher aggregation, and data-free distillation—and combined KD with other compression methods such as quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical results show that well-designed distillation can yield compact models that approach the accuracy of large pre-trained models while offering substantial savings in parameters, latency, and computational cost. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, coping with limited or unavailable training data, and selecting or weighting multiple teachers per example. The literature suggests principled strategies—attention-based layer fusion, representation-level losses, teacher confidence or dynamic weighting, and synthetic-data generation—that mitigate these issues and enable effective deployment of compressed models in domain-specific and resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Salazar
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from teacher models. A broad toolkit has emerged—matching softened outputs, aligning feature or attention maps, adversarial and online schemes, data-centric interventions (augmentation, synthetic or data-free sampling), and architecture-aware methods (pruning, quantization, or student-aware design). Practical deployment requires selecting the right signals to transfer, addressing data limitations and domain shift, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques. While distilled models often recover much of a teacher's accuracy with substantial efficiency gains, open problems remain in robustness, fairness, privacy, and principled teacher–student alignment.

papers_seen.author: Travis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression: Evidence, Mechanisms, Limits, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a central and practical toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision, generative modeling, and natural language processing. KD succeeds because it can transfer diverse signals—soft logits, intermediate representations, relational structure—and because those signals can be adapted to constraints such as data scarcity, architecture mismatch, or privacy. However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align layers, how to prepare or synthesize data, and how to address teacher errors and optimization instabilities. The best outcomes arise from integrated distillation pipelines that combine representation-level objectives, careful data strategies (including augmentation or synthetic samples), architecture-aware mapping, and multi-stage or multi-teacher schedules tailored to the deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing compact, deployable deep models by transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller students. KD operates at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational signals) and composes naturally with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on deliberate design choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, which data (real, augmented, or synthetic) to use, and how to mitigate harms such as transferred bias or degraded rare-token behavior. When integrated into a task-aware pipeline—combining pretraining, multi-level distillation objectives, projector/mapper layers, and data-side interventions—KD frequently yields students that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are widely used to transfer predictive behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. A broad family of methods—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and layer-level mimicry, multi-teacher fusion, online and teacher-free protocols, and data-free or privacy-aware synthesis—has been developed and evaluated across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Empirical studies show that, when designed carefully (teacher selection, data strategy, and objective choice), KD can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling practical deployment; however, limitations remain around domain shift, robustness, preservation of fine-grained behaviors, and data- or architecture-mismatch, motivating hybrid strategies that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware training.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring information from one or more teacher models to a student model. Methods range from matching output distributions (soft logits) to aligning internal representations, using ensembles or multiple teachers, conducting distillation without access to original data, and employing self-distillation or teacher-adaptation strategies. Empirical work across vision and language shows that careful choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to manage data constraints determine the trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. KD operates through multiple mechanisms—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations, and transferring relational or attention patterns—and often yields substantial improvements in latency, memory, and deployability relative to naive student training. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability and privacy constraints, and whether complementary compression methods are applied. Viewed as a toolbox rather than a single recipe, KD enables flexible, task-aware compression pipelines that can be adapted to real-world constraints while acknowledging remaining limits around robustness, data-free operation, and principled teacher selection.

papers_seen.author: Oneill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has developed into a flexible, practical toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in NLP and other modalities. KD methods transfer information ranging from softened output distributions to intermediate representations and relational structure, and they are commonly combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). Empirical work shows distilled students can often approach teacher performance while greatly reducing inference cost, but success depends on design choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to prepare data, and how to mitigate teacher errors, capacity mismatch, and distributional shifts. This synthesis summarizes prevailing mechanisms, typical workflows, empirical findings, limits, and practical recommendations for applying KD in production-oriented NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. A broad repertoire of KD techniques transfers information via softened outputs, intermediate-feature or attention matching, and relational or layer-wise alignment, and these techniques are commonly combined with data augmentation, teacher schedules, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but its effectiveness depends on student capacity, teacher quality, data availability and distributional match, and optimization protocols. Best practice treats KD as a flexible toolkit to be adapted to deployment constraints rather than a single fixed recipe; key open challenges include theoretical understanding, robust distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, and preserving fairness and rare-behavior fidelity during compression.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large, high-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, more efficient models (students). Across vision and language, practitioners combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, architectural design, and quantization) and with strategies for scarce or missing data to obtain deployable models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical success depends on choices about what to transfer (soft targets, features, attention), how to align heterogeneous architectures, the role of pre-training for compact models, and mechanisms to preserve robustness and rare-token behaviors. Data-free distillation, multi-task or multi-teacher schemes, and targeted representation matching extend KD’s applicability to many real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural knowledge. Methods span matching softened output distributions, feature- and attention-level imitation, layer mapping and progressive module replacement, channel- and module-aware transfers, and data-free or generative approaches for when original training data are unavailable. Practical pipelines combine KD with quantization, low-precision training, pruning, or architecture transformations and often rely on staged or adaptive teacher-student schedules. Empirical evidence shows KD can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across vision and NLP tasks, but success depends on teacher quality, what and which samples are distilled, data availability, and careful engineering of interfaces between heterogeneous teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Tool for Compression, Adaptation, and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for transferring capabilities from large or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or modality-limited models. When combined with complementary strategies—domain adaptation, feature-level matching, data augmentation, and meta-learning—distillation enables practical deployment across constrained devices, heterogeneous federated systems, and domain-shifted settings. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization subtleties and mismatches between teacher and student require methodological care and, in some cases, alternative regularization strategies.

papers_seen.author: Hardy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Task-Aware Engine for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach that should serve as the central mechanism for compressing large deep models into deployable students when matched to task constraints. KD is not a single recipe: it spans soft-target supervision, intermediate-representation matching, relational objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and data-aware or data-free protocols. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pretraining of compact models, pruning, quantization, and architecture search) and when practitioners attend to data provenance, teacher–student alignment, and robustness/fairness risks, KD routinely produces compact models that retain much of teacher performance. Best practice emphasizes task-aware design, careful selection of distillation signals, and explicit interventions for domain shift, privacy, and rare-event behavior.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Roles, Limits, and Best Practices for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly framed as a route to compress large models into smaller deployable students, but its benefits and pitfalls extend well beyond mere parameter reduction. KD acts as a form of learned regularization, can be applied in self-distillation and teacher-free regimes, and enables transferring properties such as robustness, privacy-preserving signals, and task-specific intermediate knowledge. At the same time, KD faces optimization and representation-mismatch challenges and can propagate undesirable biases from teacher to student. This paper argues that practitioners should treat KD as a flexible toolbox: combine soft-label supervision with internal-representation matching, flexible layer-mapping, attention-guided feature alignment, and targeted interventions for fairness, privacy, and robustness to get consistent benefits in both vision and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Bentley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep and NLP Models: Central Tool, Not a Panacea
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) efficiently transfers predictive behavior from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD methods range from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate representation mimicry and self- or multi-teacher schedules. While distillation often recovers much of a teacher's performance, its practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, student capacity and architecture, access to teacher data, and problem-specific constraints. Consequently, KD should be treated as a core component of a broader compression strategy that integrates architecture adaptation, data and augmentation strategies, robustness-aware training, and fairness or privacy protections.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Solis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and/or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate representation imitation, layer-wise mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, adversarial or generator-based sample synthesis, and architecture-aware adjustments—that is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and data strategies to meet deployment constraints. Empirical results show distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, but open problems remain around robustness, low-frequency behavior, teacher errors, data scarcity, and principled curricula for multi-source transfer.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Not Sufficient Tool for Compression and Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling substantial runtime, memory, and latency gains while preserving much of predictive performance. KD is effective across modalities and deployment regimes, but its success depends on careful method choice, teacher quality, data availability, and combination with complementary compression strategies. Future progress requires deeper theoretical understanding, better automation for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive settings, and principled integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool Beyond Simple Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be understood and applied as a flexible toolbox rather than merely a compression trick. KD enables compression, regularization, privacy-preserving transfer, and adaptation across diverse constraints (data scarcity, heterogeneous devices, federated settings). Effective practice combines soft-target supervision with representation-level alignment, architecture-aware methods (pruning, quantization, search), and privacy-aware or teacher-free variants. However, careful design is required to avoid capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors, and robustness or bias degradation.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Toolbox: Principles, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation should be understood and applied as a flexible set of techniques that go well beyond simple parameter compression. When treated as a toolbox—combining soft-target supervision, internal representation matching, layer-aware alignment, attention-guided mapping, and complementary compression methods—distillation can produce compact models that preserve accuracy, improve interpretability, and transfer robustness or privacy properties. Success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to prepare the student, and how to mitigate propagation of teacher defects; practitioners benefit from system-level designs that pair distillation objectives with pre-training, data augmentation, and architecture-aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Weiss
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a multifaceted toolkit that transfers information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving performance. KD operates across multiple signal levels — softened outputs, intermediate representations, and relational or attention patterns — and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). Its practical success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability or privacy constraints, and architectural mapping; when designed carefully, KD enables compact models that closely approach teacher performance but does not automatically mitigate issues like transferred biases, rare-token degradation, or distributional robustness problems.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, production-oriented family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints by trading modest amounts of accuracy for substantial reductions in compute and footprint. When treated as an engineering toolkit—combining output-level supervision, intermediate-representation transfer, multi-teacher fusion, and data-aware strategies—KD reliably produces compact models that meet real-world constraints; success requires careful matching of distillation signals to student capacity and attention to optimization, data selection, and robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in NLP: Capabilities, Extensions, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep learning models for NLP and related domains. When combined with complementary strategies—pretraining of compact models, layer-matching techniques, targeted data augmentation, robustness-aware objectives, privacy-aware protocols, and adaptive teacher training—distillation can produce small models that retain much of the teacher's accuracy while meeting deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are central tools for converting large, high-performing deep models into smaller, faster models that are practical for deployment. A broad repertoire of methods exists—matching soft logits, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial and online co-training, and data- or task-aware augmentation—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical evidence shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, but success depends on how teacher signals are represented, what data are used, and how architecture or domain mismatches are addressed. Practical deployment requires attention to data availability, privacy or federated constraints, teacher errors, and optimization stability; promising directions include pre-training compact students, online and federated distillation protocols, and specialized layer- or modality-aware objectives.

papers_seen.author: Dean
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behaviors and internal signals. A broad family of KD methods—logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, multi-teacher aggregation, and data- or task-aware variants—has been applied across vision and language tasks. Practical deployment typically combines KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and requires attention to data availability, teacher–student alignment, and robustness or fairness concerns. Open challenges include principled handling of teacher errors, data-free distillation, and reliable transfer of robustness and fairness properties.

papers_seen.author: Robertson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Flexible Toolkit for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a composable toolkit rather than a single recipe: by transferring teacher signals at multiple levels, combining input-side strategies, and integrating complementary compression methods, KD enables compact models that meet practical deployment constraints. Effective distillation requires attention to teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices about what to transfer. When deployed with these design principles, KD substantially narrows the performance gap between large teachers and efficient students while remaining adaptable to privacy, federated, and heterogeneous-device settings.
