papers_seen.author: Mcguire
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural knowledge. Across vision, language, retrieval, and graph domains, KD is a flexible toolkit that—when combined with data strategies and complementary compression techniques—enables substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while preserving much of teacher performance. Practical application requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred errors or privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—language understanding, machine translation, reading comprehension, and large-scale distributed training—recent work shows KD can improve inference speed, aid domain adaptation, enable training without original data, and increase robustness. Combining innovations in layer mapping, feature-level transfer, online and data-free techniques, and teacher optimization yields the best trade-offs for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from large, often overparameterized teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving performance. Across modalities and tasks, KD has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a diverse toolkit that includes intermediate representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, data-centric strategies (augmentation, data-free synthesis), online and distributed protocols, and task-aware adaptations. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how the student is initialized (including whether it is pre-trained), how the data distribution is shaped during distillation, and how robustness and rare-token behavior are addressed. Combining complementary techniques (pretraining, feature imitation, data mixing, and adaptive teacher strategies) produces compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints, but open issues remain around teacher selection, distributional mismatch, fairness, and adversarial robustness.

papers_seen.author: Lawson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible engineering paradigm for producing compact models from large teachers. When treated as a configurable toolkit—choosing what teacher signals to transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational structure), how to align teacher and student architectures, and which data- or curriculum-driven strategies to use—KD enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while often preserving most of the teacher's task performance. Effective deployment requires pairing distillation with complementary compression methods, pretraining or adaptation of compact architectures, and explicit attention to limits such as capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, higher-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). In practice KD has been applied to compress large pre-trained language models, enable fast inference in NLP, adapt models to new domains or tasks, support heterogeneous and federated settings, and enable data-free scenarios. Approaches differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single vs multi-teacher, jointly trained teachers), and how training data is used or synthesized. Empirical results show KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of task performance, but success depends on choices around layer mapping, feature vs. logit supervision, data complexity, and training protocols. Open challenges include handling data heterogeneity, optimizing teacher-student pairings, and ensuring stable distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Design-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a flexible toolbox—combining softened-output supervision with representation-level alignment, teacher design, and complementary compression techniques—KD reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, KD is not automatic: its success depends on what is distilled, student capacity, data availability, and targeted interventions to address robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression and Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick but a core engineering technique that enables deployment, adaptation, privacy, and robustness for large neural models in real-world systems. By treating distillation as a family of methods—ranging from output soft-target transfer to feature- and layer-wise alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols—practitioners can compress models while preserving task performance and satisfying latency, memory, and data-privacy constraints. Thoughtful application of KD, combined with complementary methods (pretraining, projector design, multi-stage schedules, and careful handling of teacher imperfections), yields compact models that are practical for production while exposing clear avenues for further research.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. KD enables practical trade-offs among accuracy, latency, privacy, and data availability by varying what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps), how it is transferred (layer-wise, channel-wise, adversarial), and which complementary compression strategies are applied (pruning, architecture search, quantization). When combined with techniques for limited or absent access to original training data, KD supports few-shot, zero-shot, and privacy-respecting workflows that make deployment feasible across modalities and resource constraints. Successful application requires selecting appropriate distilled signals and curricula, and often integrating KD with task- and architecture-specific methods.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis and Practical Takeaways
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a multi-faceted toolkit for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models to meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy) while retaining much of task performance. KD methods include soft-target (logit) matching, alignment of intermediate representations, attention- or relation-based objectives, multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware or data-free strategies. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when the distillation recipe is tailored to student capacity, data regime, and downstream robustness or fairness requirements. Open problems include reliable distillation without original data, principled handling of teacher errors and biases, and transferring robustness and rare-behavior performance to compact students.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from a teacher. A broad family of distillation objectives has been developed—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational or ensemble transfers, online and multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware approaches. Distillation is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when the distillation recipe is matched to student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical limits remain around teacher–student mismatch, preservation of low-frequency behaviors in language tasks, robustness and adversarial vulnerabilities, and privacy/communication trade-offs in federated or data-limited settings. Addressing these requires student-aware teacher design, feature- and attention-aware objectives, careful data strategies (augmentation or synthesis), and combined compression pipelines tailored to the production environment.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a diverse toolkit for transferring information from larger, more expensive models to smaller, faster, or more constrained models. Methods range from matching output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, altering training curricula, and designing compression-aware teachers or architectures. These approaches have been applied across domains including vision, speech, translation, retrieval, and on-device deployment, and have been adapted to privacy- and communication-constrained settings. Empirical and analytical work has clarified different mechanisms by which distillation aids learning, and recent work explores automation, adversarial feature transfer, sample selection, and architecture-aware strategies to improve efficiency without sacrificing much performance.

papers_seen.author: Santana
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students for deployment in resource-constrained settings. The literature shows a spectrum of distillation objectives—from matching soft output distributions to transferring intermediate representations, relational statistics, and task-specific features—and emphasizes combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free distillation). Successful distillation pipelines attend to teacher–student capacity alignment, layer- and signal-selection, and data provenance to preserve accuracy, robustness, and domain suitability. Remaining challenges include distillation without original data, robustness under distribution shift or adversarial attack, and automated, architecture-agnostic distillation for heterogeneous deployment environments.

papers_seen.author: Gross
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under constraints of memory, latency, or privacy. KD operates at multiple levels — softened output distributions, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals — and is routinely combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (use of original, augmented, synthesized, or no data). Empirical work across speech, vision, and language shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when teacher–student alignment, appropriate distillation signals, and suitable training data are carefully chosen. However, KD has predictable failure modes (capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to data heterogeneity) that require engineering choices and sometimes additional methods to obtain robust, fair, and hardware-aware compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Contextual Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible family of methods for transferring knowledge from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD techniques range from matching softened outputs to aligning intermediate representations and attention, and they can be combined with data strategies, multi-teacher schedules, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). While KD often preserves much of a teacher’s performance and enables real-world deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, its success depends on principled choices about what signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, how to obtain or synthesize distillation data, and how to mitigate optimization and robustness limits. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a configurable, task-aware system rather than a single recipe, and it provides practical recommendations for designing effective distillation pipelines in NLP and related deep-learning domains.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Conditional Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach for converting large models into smaller, deployable ones. By transferring softened outputs, intermediate representations, relational structure, and ensemble behavior — and by combining distillation with complementary methods like pruning, quantization, and architecture search — KD enables substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of a teacher’s performance. However, its effectiveness depends on design choices: what signals are distilled, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability or synthesis, and explicit handling of robustness, fairness, and domain shift. Treating KD as a configurable, system-level toolkit rather than a single recipe yields the most reliable path to compact, high-quality models for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Methods, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring behavioral and representational signals from teachers. KD includes diverse techniques — soft-target supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer-mapping strategies, online and ensemble-to-single transfers, and selective sample or data-aware procedures — that are adapted to task, architecture, and deployment constraints. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and appropriate data strategies, KD can yield compact models that retain most teacher performance; however, success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, and data availability.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Figueroa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies condense large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or lower-precision students suitable for deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Research has produced a taxonomy of approaches—soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate/feature imitation, relational or attention-based losses, multi-teacher fusion, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates that properly designed distillation pipelines can preserve most teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling substantial gains in inference speed and memory; theoretical analyses attribute much of KD’s benefit to regularization from soft targets and the transfer of inductive biases. Remaining challenges include handling teacher–student capacity mismatch, preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors, operating without original training data, and designing adaptive, task-aware distillation signals.

papers_seen.author: Mcmillan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Adaptive Tool for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the original performance. KD's successes across vision, speech, and NLP show that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention), how to align teacher and student, and whether to rely on original data or generated/synthetic data determines outcomes. To be effective in real deployments, KD must be combined with complementary methods (data-free generation, federated protocols, targeted augmentation, and robustness-aware objectives) and applied adaptively to task and resource constraints. When used thoughtfully, KD enables substantial efficiency gains without wholesale architectural redesign; when used naively it can propagate teacher errors or exacerbate distributional and low-frequency lexical problems.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core — Powerful but Contextual in Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance when combined with complementary techniques (e.g., representation alignment, architecture-aware search, data synthesis, and multi-teacher schedules), but it is not a universal cure: data scarcity, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency/token behaviors in NLP, and fairness or privacy constraints limit its effectiveness unless practitioners design targeted, hybrid pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Dependent Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while often preserving much of the teacher's effectiveness. KD methods range from matching soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations or using adversarial generators when training data are unavailable; they have been successfully applied across vision, generative modeling, recommender systems, and large pretrained language models. However, KD’s success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to address limited or private data, robustness, and bias—so practitioners must pair KD with task-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives to get reliable, deployable results.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a versatile suite of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Modern KD extends beyond soft-label matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical deployment of distilled models depends on matching the distillation recipe to task constraints (data availability, teacher–student capacity, architecture heterogeneity, and privacy or communication limits) and frequently benefits from multi-stage or task-aware distillation schedules. While KD often yields compact models that approach teacher performance, open issues remain around capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases or errors, robustness under distribution shift, and reliable methods for distillation without original training data.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, and Context-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically proven approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. As a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD encompasses soft-targets, intermediate representation matching, attention- and layer-aware mappings, multi- and online-teacher schemes, and data-aware protocols (including data-free and few-shot variants). KD delivers strong efficiency–performance tradeoffs when paired with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, but its benefits depend on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to handle limited or private data. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central, adaptable component of compression pipelines while recognizing its limits and prescribing evidence-based design practices for robust, task-aware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. Research over the past decade has produced a wide array of distillation variants (logit-based supervision, feature and attention matching, multi- and self-distillation, data-free methods) and shown how KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet practical constraints. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both the strengths of KD (regularization, practical deployment gains, domain adaptation) and its limits (optimization difficulty, capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors), motivating a pragmatic set of design choices for robust compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Ashley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. KD works at multiple levels — soft logits, intermediate representations, relational structure, and ensemble behaviour — and is most effective when combined with data strategies, teacher–student co-design, and complementary compression such as pruning or quantization. While KD often preserves much of teacher performance and can regularize student training, its success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align capacities, and how to handle limited or mismatched data; careful, task-aware protocols are therefore essential for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-level toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. Effective KD requires selecting what to transfer (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational signals), matching teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques. When applied with task-aware objectives, projector or alignment modules, and careful treatment of data and teacher preparation, KD yields compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints, though capacity mismatch and data limitations remain important caveats.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, higher-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). In practice KD has been applied to compress large pre-trained language models, enable fast inference in NLP, adapt models to new domains or tasks, support heterogeneous and federated settings, and enable data-free scenarios. Approaches differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single vs multi-teacher, jointly trained teachers), and how training data is used or synthesized. Empirical results show KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of task performance, but success depends on choices around layer mapping, feature vs. logit supervision, data complexity, and training protocols. Open challenges include handling data heterogeneity, optimizing teacher-student pairings, and ensuring stable distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deploying large pretrained models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from high-capacity teachers to smaller students. Methods include transferring softened output distributions, matching intermediate features or attention maps, layer- and task-aware alignment, online and mutual distillation, and data-free approaches that synthesize surrogate inputs. Empirical evidence across vision and language tasks shows that well-designed distillation can preserve most teacher performance while substantially reducing model size, latency, and energy use. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to map heterogeneous architectures, and how to handle limited or private data. Remaining challenges center on preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence models, avoiding transfer of biases or adversarial vulnerabilities, and jointly optimizing compression for hardware and task constraints.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a multifaceted toolkit for shrinking large neural models while retaining much of their accuracy. Approaches include matching teacher outputs (soft logits), aligning intermediate representations or attention patterns, transforming architectures to be resource-efficient, and designing teacher–student curricula or multi-teacher aggregations. KD is applied across supervised, self-supervised, few-shot, federated, and privacy-constrained scenarios and is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align layers and capacity, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; when designed carefully, KD enables deployment of compact models for diverse NLP and vision tasks while exposing open questions about robustness, fairness, and distributional generalization.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Alexander
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Context-Dependent Toolbox for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible engineering toolbox that enables deploying large models as compact students under constraints of compute, latency, and data privacy. In practice KD operates at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational signals), can be combined with data augmentation or synthetic-data generators, and integrates with complementary compression methods such as pruning and quantization. While KD often preserves much of teacher performance and provides useful regularization, its effectiveness depends on choices about distillation targets, teacher preparation, student architecture, and data strategy; it can also propagate teacher biases or fail under severe domain mismatch. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a system—selecting appropriate signals, preparing teachers and students, using synthetic or privacy-aware data methods when necessary, and validating robustness and fairness in the target environment.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for creating smaller, faster models from larger ones while retaining much of their functionality. When combined with representation matching, architecture-aware surgery, selective sample strategies, and privacy-aware protocols, KD enables deployment of high-quality models across modalities and constrained environments. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; without such care, distillation can underperform or transfer undesirable behaviors. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central, composable tool in compression toolkits, and outlines concrete methodological priorities that practitioners should follow to realize reliable, efficient distilled models.

papers_seen.author: Mccann
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring useful information from teacher models. KD encompasses multiple information channels (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational signals) and is commonly used together with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture redesign) to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to handle data (real, augmented, or synthesized). While KD often preserves much of teacher performance and can serve additional roles such as regularization, domain adaptation, and privacy-aware model release, it has predictable failure modes—capacity mismatch, domain shift, and propagation of teacher errors—that necessitate careful pipeline design and complementary methods for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Riggs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring information from a teacher in the form of softened outputs, intermediate representations, or relational structure. Over the past decade KD has matured into a flexible toolkit that is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-synthesis strategies to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, but success depends strongly on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data and optimization are handled. Remaining limitations include capacity and optimization mismatches, degradation on low-frequency or domain-specific behaviors, and risk of transferring teacher biases or vulnerabilities.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a set of teacher→student techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving students. Across vision and NLP, KD variants include soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and feature-level imitation, relational or structure-preserving losses, multi-teacher ensembles, data-agnostic or data-free procedures, and self- or cross-supervised transfer. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing compact models but requires careful handling of data regimes, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and robustness or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations. Across modalities and tasks, distillation methods vary by what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate features, attention, or structural knowledge), by whether they rely on original training data, and by how the teacher-student relationship is optimized. Practical goals include reducing inference cost, preserving accuracy under domain shift, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, and improving robustness or fairness. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen transfer targets, training curricula, and data strategies can recover much of the teacher performance in compact models, and that meta-level and task-adaptive approaches further improve transfer effectiveness. Key open concerns are how to best align heterogeneous inputs or architectures, how to retain desirable inductive biases (e.g., for domain-specific tasks), and how to ensure reliable student performance without access to teacher training data.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Mcguire
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural knowledge. Across vision, language, retrieval, and graph domains, KD is a flexible toolkit that—when combined with data strategies and complementary compression techniques—enables substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while preserving much of teacher performance. Practical application requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred errors or privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or ensemble neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across computer vision, speech, multimodal, and NLP tasks, distillation protocols—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate feature and attention-based transfers—enable practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and memory. Success depends on careful choices of distillation targets, teacher-student compatibility, data availability, and training dynamics; when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, low-precision, architecture search, or federated protocols) it yields deployable models for resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple training trick into a versatile, task-aware toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD operates through multiple, complementary mechanisms—matching teacher outputs, imitating internal representations, and encoding relational or structural knowledge—and is commonly combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data-side strategies (augmentation, synthesis, or data-free approaches). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often preserves most teacher performance while providing additional benefits such as implicit regularization, domain adaptation, and improved calibration; at the same time, practical limits (student capacity, data quality, and teacher imperfections) require careful signal selection, alignment modules, and deployment-aware protocols. Remaining challenges include principled teacher selection, robust distillation under domain shift or privacy constraints, and scaling KD to heterogeneous, multimodal, or low-resource production settings.

papers_seen.author: Morrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core of Model Compression — Strengths, Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to which teacher signals are transferred, how the student is initialized, and how complementary compression methods are integrated, KD reliably reduces inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a magic bullet: theoretical and empirical work highlights optimization gaps, failures under heterogeneous data or federated settings, and robustness and rare-token fidelity issues. Realistic deployment therefore requires task-aware distillation recipes, student pre-training, data strategies (including data-free synthesis when necessary), and explicit evaluation of failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. Across vision and natural language tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, selective sample transfer, multi-teacher and data-free strategies—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving most of the teacher’s performance. Practical success depends on matching what is distilled to student capacity, managing data availability (including data-free or synthetic approaches), and addressing harms such as transferred biases or degraded rare-token behavior. A pragmatic pipeline mixes pretraining, representation-aware losses, targeted data manipulations, and teacher-aware design to achieve favorable trade-offs among efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a flexible, system-level toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD techniques transfer information ranging from softened outputs to intermediate representations and relational structure; they can be combined with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies that include augmentation, synthetic generation, or data-free approaches. Effective distillation depends on matching the distillation signals, student architecture, and data strategy to task and deployment constraints. While well-designed KD pipelines often recover most teacher performance, remaining challenges include optimization instability, transfer of teacher errors or biases, handling limited or private data, and preserving rare-token/long-tail behavior in sequence models.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a System: Practical Strengths, Limits, and Prescriptions for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a modular system—combining soft-target supervision, representation-level objectives, data augmentation, multi-teacher signals, and complementary compression methods—KD reliably yields compact models that preserve much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. Effectiveness depends on handling data availability, architecture mismatches, and undesirable teacher artifacts; these constraints are manageable when KD is designed with domain adaptation, input alignment, and augmentation-aware strategies. I argue KD should be the default toolchain for producing production-ready compact models, applied with explicit attention to what knowledge is transferred and how it is matched to student capacity and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ferguson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Composable Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated as the central, modular technique in modern model-compression pipelines: it reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller students while remaining flexible enough to combine with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-side interventions. KD’s practical success depends on deliberate choices—what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or sensitive data, and how to evaluate robustness and long-tail behavior. When used as part of a system that addresses optimization, data, and mismatch issues, KD frequently yields compact models that meet deployment constraints; when used alone or carelessly it can underperform or propagate undesirable behaviors. The remainder of this paper argues for KD as the default, central component of compression toolkits while outlining its limits and concrete design recommendations to mitigate them.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Nuanced Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for creating compact, deployable models from large teachers. When treated as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe, KD enables significant reductions in memory, compute, and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. Its success depends on careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to manage data (real, augmented, or synthesized), and how KD is integrated with complementary compression methods. KD is powerful for production constraints but must be applied with task-aware design to avoid propagating teacher weaknesses or failing under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Cooke
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) condenses larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behaviors and internal representations. Across vision, speech, NLP, and generative modeling, KD variants (soft-target/logit matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and data-free approaches) enable substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often retaining most of the teacher’s task performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, the availability or synthesis of distillation data, and integration with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Remaining challenges include principled teacher selection and weighting, data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, preserving low-frequency or fine-grained behaviors, and robustness/fairness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deploying large deep models by transferring their predictive behavior or internal structure to smaller, faster models. Research has progressed from soft-label teacher-student training toward richer objectives that match internal representations, feature spaces, and decision boundaries; from data-dependent distillation to data-free and privacy-preserving approaches; and from one-size-fits-all compression to task-adaptive, architecture-aware methods. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance across speech, vision, and language tasks when distillation objectives, training data (real or synthetic), and search for efficient architectures are carefully tailored. Remaining challenges include optimization barriers that prevent perfect teacher matching, balancing regularization and fidelity, and handling heterogeneous or absent data during distillation.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. A broad repertoire of KD techniques transfers information via softened outputs, intermediate-feature or attention matching, and relational or layer-wise alignment, and these techniques are commonly combined with data augmentation, teacher schedules, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but its effectiveness depends on student capacity, teacher quality, data availability and distributional match, and optimization protocols. Best practice treats KD as a flexible toolkit to be adapted to deployment constraints rather than a single fixed recipe; key open challenges include theoretical understanding, robust distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, and preserving fairness and rare-behavior fidelity during compression.

papers_seen.author: Ware
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical System for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and practical approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a system—covering teacher design, the training signal, data and augmentation, and efficiency constraints—KD can retain much of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and domain requirements. However, its success depends on careful choices about teacher quality, distillation objectives, available data, and complementary compression techniques; awareness of these factors yields the most reliable compressed models.
