papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Responses
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural signals. Across vision and NLP, KD variants—logit/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, multi- and self-teaching, and combinations with pruning/quantization—enable reduced inference cost and on-device deployment while attempting to retain performance. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD acts both as a route to transfer representational inductive biases and as a form of learned regularization; its success depends on signal choice, data provenance, capacity mismatch, and optimization. Methodological refinements (data augmentation, adversarial or boundary-focused examples, data-free synthesis, teacher design, and divergence choices) address core challenges in practice, but open problems remain around robustness, privacy, fairness, and reliably closing the teacher–student performance gap.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable deep models across vision and natural language tasks. KD encompasses matching teacher outputs, aligning internal representations, leveraging multi-teacher or online schedules, and using data-side strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). When combined with architecture-aware design and complementary compression methods, KD often yields students that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Remaining challenges center on teacher–student mismatch, data availability, robustness, and the potential transfer of undesirable biases.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Empirical, Theoretical, and Practical Advances
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools to reduce the size and latency of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Research has produced a diverse set of KD variants — offline teacher-student distillation, multi-teacher and two-stage schemes, online/distillation-in-training, self-distillation, and combinations with pruning — and has demonstrated practical impact across NLP (e.g., translation, question answering, language modeling) and other domains. Work has also begun to explain when and why distillation helps, pointing to effects on data complexity, bias–variance tradeoffs, and the distribution of learned representations across network layers. Implementation-oriented studies emphasize efficient pipelines (to avoid repeated teacher forward passes), dataset-level filtering, and the complementary role of structured pruning for deployment on constrained hardware. Together, these findings show KD is both a pragmatic engineering tool and a growing subject of theoretical understanding, with ongoing research addressing teacher imperfection, optimal training signal mixes, and scalability to very large datasets or distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Gross
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under constraints of memory, latency, or privacy. KD operates at multiple levels — softened output distributions, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals — and is routinely combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (use of original, augmented, synthesized, or no data). Empirical work across speech, vision, and language shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when teacher–student alignment, appropriate distillation signals, and suitable training data are carefully chosen. However, KD has predictable failure modes (capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to data heterogeneity) that require engineering choices and sometimes additional methods to obtain robust, fair, and hardware-aware compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible set of methods for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can meet practical deployment constraints. KD yields strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks when practitioners choose appropriate distillation signals, address teacher–student alignment, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques. However, its success is conditional: student capacity, the quality and availability of data used for distillation, optimization dynamics, and inherited teacher biases can all limit outcomes. Effective compression therefore treats KD as a toolbox to be adapted to task requirements rather than a single recipe, pairing it with architecture-aware compression, data and sample strategies, and careful evaluation of robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Practical Directions for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compress large models into lightweight students for deployment. Recent work shows that KD can preserve most of a teacher's performance while dramatically reducing model size or computational cost, but gains depend on what knowledge is transferred, how teachers and students are prepared, and the distillation protocol. I argue that (1) transferring richer information than final logits, (2) preparing students with pre-training, (3) augmenting or synthesizing data during distillation, and (4) co-optimizing architecture-aware compression with distillation together form a robust recipe for reliable compression in NLP and other domains. These directions address generalization, data scarcity, and architectural differences, and they are supported by recent empirical and methodological studies across speech, vision, retrieval, and language modeling.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: The Case for Practical, Adaptive Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible tool for compressing large deep learning models into deployable students. Recent work shows KD can both directly reduce model size and serve as a mechanism to transfer inductive biases, intermediate representations, and task-specific attention. However, real-world constraints — limited or private training data, domain and client heterogeneity, and redundant teacher representations — require KD methods that are data-free, adversarially robust, task-aware, and selective about what teacher knowledge to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core of Model Compression: Effectiveness, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and NLP. When combined with complementary practices—task-aware signal selection, intermediate representation alignment, pretraining for compact architectures, multi-teacher or self-distillation, and data augmentation or synthesis—KD can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: data availability, teacher–student heterogeneity, fairness concerns, and theoretical gaps constrain its effectiveness in some settings. Careful design choices and hybrid pipelines are therefore required to realize reliable compression in production systems.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Methods, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or costly models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Research over the past decade shows multiple complementary mechanisms for effective distillation—soft-target supervision, feature and representation mimicking, layer-wise alignment, and task-aware selection of teacher knowledge. Practical advances adapt distillation to domain constraints (few-shot data, modality mismatch, federated or latency-constrained deployment) and model families (transformers, convolutional nets, graph neural networks, generative models). Empirical work demonstrates that thoughtful choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features vs. relations), how to align layers, and how to prepare data and pretraining substantially affect student performance, sometimes enabling students to match or even surpass teachers under resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. The literature has expanded beyond soft-label matching to include intermediate representation imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and adaptive-teacher schemes, data- and domain-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning or architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can preserve a large fraction of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, while theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when distillation helps, how teacher quality and data regimes affect outcomes, and what practical trade-offs remain. Open problems center on robustness to domain shift and adversaries, distillation without original data, and automated, architecture-agnostic pipelines for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while attempting to retain performance. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD variants address constraints such as limited computation, on-device heterogeneity, lack of access to teacher training data, fairness concerns, and the need for task-specific efficiency. Common themes include transferring softened output distributions, matching intermediate representations, using multiple teachers or self-generated targets, and integrating compression with architecture search or pre-training. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact, practical models for deployment, but also reveals optimization and data-dependence limitations that motivate method refinements like task-adaptive search, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, and self-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster student models suitable for resource-constrained deployment. A diverse set of strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and intermediate representation matching to multi-teacher ensembles, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-supervised or privacy-preserving protocols—have been developed to preserve accuracy, robustness, and modality transfer while reducing inference cost. Practical systems combine distillation with quantization, pruning, or architecture search to meet application-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and intermediate representations. Across vision, speech, language, and graph modalities, KD methods exploit soft targets, feature- and attention-level alignment, contrastive and adversarial objectives, and architecture-aware design to trade accuracy for latency, memory, or privacy. Practical success depends on choices about teacher-student design, data availability and quality, and optimization strategies; contemporary work emphasizes combining representation-level objectives, teacher-friendly or teacher-free approaches, and data-aware training to produce robust, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Conditional
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. KD operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate features, relational signals) and is most effective when integrated with complementary practices such as pre-training, architecture-aware design, data-side strategies, and other compression techniques. However, its success is conditional on deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or mismatched data, and how to mitigate propagation of teacher errors or biases. Treating KD as a flexible toolkit rather than a single recipe yields the best results for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Necessary Precautions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach for turning large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students. As a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD transfers predictive behavior and internal structure via soft targets, intermediate-feature alignment, attention maps, and relational objectives. When integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with careful data and architecture design, KD routinely yields compact models that preserve much of teacher performance and enable latency-, memory-, or privacy-constrained deployment. However, KD’s benefits are contingent on student capacity, data availability and provenance, teacher artifacts, and distributional shift; addressing these requires deliberate, task-aware pipelines and evaluation tailored to real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a set of techniques that transfer knowledge from larger, expensive models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students) so the students retain much of the teacher utility while fitting deployment constraints. Research has produced a variety of distillation paradigms: logit- and soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, layer-wise and channel-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, self-supervised distillation, multi-teacher ensembles and domain-aware adaptation. Empirical work shows that combining pre-training for compact architectures with distillation, using task-aware selection of teacher signals, and tailoring distillation to modality- or task-specific structure leads to stronger compressed models. Important open issues include distillation without access to original data, preserving fairness and privacy in compressed models, and closing the capacity gap between teacher and student without over-constraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Multifaceted Strategy for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep and NLP models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. Beyond matching final outputs, modern KD variants transfer intermediate representations, adapt teacher behavior to students, and operate when task data are limited or unavailable. KD is most effective when combined with task-aware signal selection, teacher design, data strategies, and complementary compression such as architecture search or pruning; used in this way, KD enables compact models that approach teacher performance while addressing real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, and Evolving Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core engineering and research paradigm for compressing large models into efficient students while preserving accuracy and desirable behaviors. KD encompasses soft-target transfer, intermediate representation alignment, ensemble-to-single compression, and complementary data- and architecture-aware techniques. When treated as a design problem—choosing which signals to transfer, how to align representations, and how to manage data constraints—KD enables deployment across resource-limited and domain-shifted settings, but open challenges remain in preserving rare-token behaviors, coping with imperfect teachers, and operating without original data.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. A family of methods—matching teacher soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, transferring relational structure, and synthesizing or selecting data—enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Success in real systems depends on task-aware design, careful teacher–student pairing, handling limited or private data, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. Research over the past decade has produced a wide array of distillation variants (logit-based supervision, feature and attention matching, multi- and self-distillation, data-free methods) and shown how KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet practical constraints. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both the strengths of KD (regularization, practical deployment gains, domain adaptation) and its limits (optimization difficulty, capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors), motivating a pragmatic set of design choices for robust compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from matching teacher logits to a flexible toolkit for producing compact, efficient models suitable for deployment and adaptation in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can transfer predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and task-specific properties (e.g., robustness or privacy signals), and it is most effective when combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, data-side interventions, and low-precision or structured pruning. Success depends on careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, how to construct or augment distillation data, and how to adapt teacher behavior; practical pipelines treat KD as one component of a broader compression workflow rather than a universal solution.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Patton
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or costly neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. A convergent literature shows a spectrum of distillation objectives (soft-targets, intermediate representations, attention and relational signals), a set of practical integrations with pruning, quantization and architecture search, and a set of recurring challenges: teacher–student capacity mismatch, limited or unavailable distillation data, and robustness under domain shift or adversarial influence. Effective pipelines attend to student initialization (including pre-training), careful choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and targeted data strategies (augmentation or synthetic data) to achieve deployable compressed models while managing performance, fairness and privacy trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical Tool for Compression — Powerful When Combined, Limited When Used Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller students that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD spans soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention alignment, multi-teacher schedules, and many-to-many layer mapping. In practice, KD reliably improves student efficiency and often preserves much of teacher behavior, but it has predictable failure modes — e.g., propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to teacher–student mismatch, and dependence on data quality and augmentation — that require complementary practices such as student pretraining, careful teacher design, data augmentation, and hybrid compression (pruning/quantization).

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or ensemble models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. It is used to reduce memory, compute, and latency for deployment, to enable low-precision inference, to protect privacy, and to adapt models across domains. Practical distillation methods vary in what is transferred (logits, features, relations), how teachers are chosen (single, multi-teacher, self), and how training is regularized (data augmentation, loss design, adversarial objectives). While distillation often yields students that outperform similarly sized models trained from scratch, mismatches between teacher and student, optimization difficulties, and domain/privacy constraints remain important concerns. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and language tasks shows that careful design choices (data augmentation, multi-stage distillation, private/noisy queries, and specialized losses) meaningfully affect student performance and deployment trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Flores
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad ecosystem of KD variants has emerged—matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate features or attention, transferring relational structure, online and multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware techniques. In practice KD is often combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data-management strategies to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. While KD routinely enables large reductions in parameters and inference cost with modest drops in accuracy, challenges remain in handling domain shift, limited or private data, preserving rare-token or fine-grained behaviors, and avoiding propagation of teacher errors and biases.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-level toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. Effective KD requires selecting what to transfer (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational signals), matching teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques. When applied with task-aware objectives, projector or alignment modules, and careful treatment of data and teacher preparation, KD yields compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints, though capacity mismatch and data limitations remain important caveats.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, higher-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). In practice KD has been applied to compress large pre-trained language models, enable fast inference in NLP, adapt models to new domains or tasks, support heterogeneous and federated settings, and enable data-free scenarios. Approaches differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single vs multi-teacher, jointly trained teachers), and how training data is used or synthesized. Empirical results show KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of task performance, but success depends on choices around layer mapping, feature vs. logit supervision, data complexity, and training protocols. Open challenges include handling data heterogeneity, optimizing teacher-student pairings, and ensuring stable distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Hardy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Task-Aware Engine for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach that should serve as the central mechanism for compressing large deep models into deployable students when matched to task constraints. KD is not a single recipe: it spans soft-target supervision, intermediate-representation matching, relational objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and data-aware or data-free protocols. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pretraining of compact models, pruning, quantization, and architecture search) and when practitioners attend to data provenance, teacher–student alignment, and robustness/fairness risks, KD routinely produces compact models that retain much of teacher performance. Best practice emphasizes task-aware design, careful selection of distillation signals, and explicit interventions for domain shift, privacy, and rare-event behavior.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a set of teacher→student techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving students. Across vision and NLP, KD variants include soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and feature-level imitation, relational or structure-preserving losses, multi-teacher ensembles, data-agnostic or data-free procedures, and self- or cross-supervised transfer. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing compact models but requires careful handling of data regimes, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and robustness or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compressing and Adapting Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Across settings—domain adaptation, resource-constrained deployment, privacy-limited releases, sequence generation, and large-scale distributed training—distillation methods enable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and cost. By leveraging teacher signals (soft targets, feature representations, or ensembles), self-distillation, and data- or communication-efficient protocols, practitioners can tailor compression strategies to meet production constraints without wholesale redesign of model architectures.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and a Task-Aware Prescription
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective engine for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and NLP. KD’s flexibility—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, using multi-teacher schedules, and operating with or without original data—makes it the practical backbone of compression pipelines. However, distillation can amplify teacher biases, struggle with rare-token or long-tail behavior, and depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; practitioners should therefore adopt integrated, task-aware KD workflows combined with complementary compression techniques and explicit evaluation of failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Santana
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students for deployment in resource-constrained settings. The literature shows a spectrum of distillation objectives—from matching soft output distributions to transferring intermediate representations, relational statistics, and task-specific features—and emphasizes combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free distillation). Successful distillation pipelines attend to teacher–student capacity alignment, layer- and signal-selection, and data provenance to preserve accuracy, robustness, and domain suitability. Remaining challenges include distillation without original data, robustness under distribution shift or adversarial attack, and automated, architecture-agnostic distillation for heterogeneous deployment environments.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.
