papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger, higher-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other learned structure. Across NLP and broader deep-learning tasks, a family of techniques—logit/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, layer-wise mapping, multi-teacher and ensemble transfer, and data-free or generator-based synthesis—enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Distillation is both a practical engineering toolkit for deployment constraints (latency, memory, heterogeneity, privacy) and an active research area that raises challenges around preserving robustness, handling domain and data shifts, and designing principled curricula and teacher signals for maximal downstream utility.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Methods, Practical Patterns, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compacts large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structured relational signals. A broad set of techniques—soft-target matching, representation- and attention-level alignment, multi-teacher schedules, self- or data-free distillation, and integration with pruning/quantization or architecture adaptation—enables large reductions in latency and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. Success depends on what knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate data; predictable failure modes include capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and transfer of teacher errors or biases. Practical deployment treats KD as an engineering toolkit that must be adapted to task, data, and hardware constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Dependent Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while often preserving much of the teacher's effectiveness. KD methods range from matching soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations or using adversarial generators when training data are unavailable; they have been successfully applied across vision, generative modeling, recommender systems, and large pretrained language models. However, KD’s success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to address limited or private data, robustness, and bias—so practitioners must pair KD with task-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives to get reliable, deployable results.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a System: Practical Strengths, Limits, and Prescriptions for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a modular system—combining soft-target supervision, representation-level objectives, data augmentation, multi-teacher signals, and complementary compression methods—KD reliably yields compact models that preserve much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. Effectiveness depends on handling data availability, architecture mismatches, and undesirable teacher artifacts; these constraints are manageable when KD is designed with domain adaptation, input alignment, and augmentation-aware strategies. I argue KD should be the default toolchain for producing production-ready compact models, applied with explicit attention to what knowledge is transferred and how it is matched to student capacity and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Dixon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods compress large deep models into smaller, faster, or more private models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature shows a spectrum of KD signals (soft logits, intermediate features, layer mappings), enhancements via data interventions and architecture search, and combinations with pruning or low-precision inference. Practical success depends on task- and deployment-aware choices (which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, what augmentations or synthetic data to use) as well as attention to privacy and robustness. The field has produced effective recipes for compressing pretrained language models, vision transformers, and generative models, while ongoing work clarifies limits and complementary techniques for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Design-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a flexible toolbox—combining softened-output supervision with representation-level alignment, teacher design, and complementary compression techniques—KD reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, KD is not automatic: its success depends on what is distilled, student capacity, data availability, and targeted interventions to address robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. The technique has diversified into a family of methods (logit matching, feature- and layer-level imitation, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free and federated variants) and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, pretraining, and augmentation to meet deployment constraints. Practical success depends on matching distillation strategy to goals (latency, privacy, robustness) and on careful handling of teacher quality, student capacity, and available data.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, practical paradigm for compressing large models into compact students for deployment in deep learning and NLP. When applied as a toolkit—combining softened-output supervision, internal-feature matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation schedules, and data strategies including data-free synthesis—KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while recovering much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a panacea: success requires careful matching of teacher signals to student capacity, attention to domain shift and low-frequency behaviors, and integration with robustness- and privacy-preserving practices. This paper argues for principled, hybrid KD workflows that pair representation-aware objectives, thoughtful data strategies, and complementary compression techniques to produce reliable, deployment-ready models.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core technique for producing compact, deployable neural models by transferring predictive behavior or internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller students. KD encompasses a spectrum of objectives — from matching soft output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, relational statistics, or task-specific features — and it is often combined with architectural modification, pruning, quantization, or data synthesis to meet deployment constraints. Practical KD addresses data scarcity, domain shift, heterogeneity of devices and architectures, and privacy concerns through strategies such as data-free distillation, multi-teacher weighting, teacher adaptation, and curriculum or instance-aware sampling. While KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss, careful design is needed to avoid capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, and degradation on rare or out-of-domain inputs.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, System-Level Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, system-level strategy for compressing large deep and NLP models into compact, deployable students. When KD is designed as a modular pipeline—combining soft-target supervision, intermediate-representation matching, selective data strategies, multi-teacher aggregation, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture surgery)—it reliably produces small models that retain much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful handling of transferred biases and domain shifts. Practical deployments therefore require principled choices about what knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data strategies to apply.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are central tools for converting large, high-performing deep models into smaller, faster models that are practical for deployment. A broad repertoire of methods exists—matching soft logits, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial and online co-training, and data- or task-aware augmentation—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical evidence shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, but success depends on how teacher signals are represented, what data are used, and how architecture or domain mismatches are addressed. Practical deployment requires attention to data availability, privacy or federated constraints, teacher errors, and optimization stability; promising directions include pre-training compact students, online and federated distillation protocols, and specialized layer- or modality-aware objectives.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Uses, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applied paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient students for deployment under compute, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. A spectrum of techniques—from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—supports a range of practical trade-offs. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing footprint, but success depends on student capacity, data availability, and careful design choices; important open problems remain around robustness, principled teacher selection, and reliable distillation under heterogeneous or private data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. While classic distillation focuses on matching teacher output probabilities, practical compression across modalities and tasks benefits from richer transfer mechanisms: aligning internal representations, selecting task-relevant signals, leveraging data augmentation or synthetic data when real data are scarce, and using adversarial or ensemble strategies to expose diverse and robust teacher knowledge. When combined thoughtfully these methods enable students that are much smaller and faster while retaining or even improving accuracy and robustness on downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central paradigm for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Research spans theoretical analyses of when and why distillation helps, practical methods for compressing pretrained language models, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, strategies to preserve robustness, and distributed/federated adaptations. Methods include soft-label matching, intermediate feature/attention imitation, many-to-many layer mappings, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-distillation. Empirical and theoretical work highlights gains in efficiency and deployment feasibility across vision and NLP tasks, while also revealing limitations related to data distribution, teacher quality, robustness, and low-frequency token coverage. Open directions include principled handling of imperfect teachers, domain adaptation during compression, robustness-aware distillation, and scalable distillation in distributed or data-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Jefferson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: A Central, Practical Tool with Clear Limits and Engineering Requirements
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique for producing compact, deployable deep models by transferring information from larger teachers to smaller students. Empirical work across vision, speech, ranking, and natural language tasks shows KD can deliver large reductions in parameter count and latency while retaining much of a teacher’s predictive power. However, KD is not an automatic solution: its success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, how the teacher is prepared, student architecture and pretraining, the provenance and augmentation of distillation data, and complementary compression techniques. Responsible deployment requires engineering KD into a broader compression pipeline that addresses data, robustness, fairness, and optimization concerns.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Methods, Limits, and Complementary Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core strategy to compress large pre-trained deep models so they can be deployed in latency- and resource-constrained settings. KD variants—multi-teacher pipelines, layer-wise and task-aware alignment, self-distillation, and feature-level matching—enable small students to approach or match teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost. KD is most effective when combined with complementary approaches such as pruning and architecture search, and when adapted to domain or system constraints (e.g., federated or multi-device settings). However, KD is not a universal panacea: data heterogeneity, misaligned inputs between teacher and student, and inappropriate augmentation or feature transfer can limit gains, so careful design choices are required to realize practical compression.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression across Modalities
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic for transferring soft logits to a rich family of techniques that enable deployment of large models in resource-constrained settings. Across NLP, vision, generative modeling, and cross-modal systems, distillation methods that match intermediate representations, adapt teacher signals to student inputs, exploit many-to-many layer correspondences, and combine with pruning or ensemble guidance consistently produce compact models with near-teacher performance. KD is also effective for domain adaptation and continual learning, making it a practical foundation for producing small, fast, and robust models for real-world applications.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Bounded Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When implemented beyond simple soft-label matching — e.g., via intermediate-feature alignment, layer-mapping, task-aware objectives, curriculum-driven sample selection, or privacy-preserving synthesis — KD can preserve much of a teacher’s performance while reducing inference cost and enabling on-device, federated, or low-latency deployment. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategy, and attention to robustness, fairness, and domain shift. Best practice treats KD as one element in a compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted evaluation for adversarial and distributional failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques reduce the size and runtime of large neural models by transferring information from one or more high-capacity teacher models to a smaller student model. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, methods vary in what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, relations, or latent experts), how training data are used (original data, distilled predictions, or no data), and how multiple or imperfect teachers are combined. Practical adaptations include task-specific losses, sample selection or weighting, and architectural transformations; KD is also integrated with system-level strategies such as federated learning and pruning to meet device constraints. Empirical results show KD can preserve much of teacher performance while substantially reducing compute and memory, but success depends on choices of teacher strength, data availability, multi-teacher aggregation, and whether task structure (e.g., localization or ranking) is explicitly addressed.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is the most practical and versatile tool available today for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as the core of a compression pipeline and combined with complementary techniques (representation alignment, data strategies, pruning/quantization, and privacy-preserving mechanisms), KD enables production-ready models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: capacity mismatch, domain shift, optimization instability, and risks of propagating teacher errors demand task-aware design, careful data handling, and hybrid engineering practices to obtain reliable results in realistic deployments.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) unifies a set of techniques that transfer information from large, accurate teacher networks into smaller, faster student models to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints. Methods vary from matching softened output distributions to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, or relational structure, and are frequently combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture redesign. Practical success depends on choices about the distillation signal, teacher–student alignment, availability and generation of training data, and optimization schedules. Across vision and language tasks, task-aware and deployment-aware distillation pipelines—often hybridizing multiple signals and synthesis or augmentation of data—produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance, though open problems remain around sample efficiency, robustness, fairness, and principled objective design.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Practical Strengths and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central engineering and research tool for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior of larger teachers. Its variants—logit matching, feature- and relation-level transfer, multi- and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware protocols—enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on design choices (what to transfer, how to align architectures, and how to handle data), and it can propagate teacher errors or undesirable behaviors unless paired with complementary techniques and careful evaluation. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a flexible, context-dependent component of compression pipelines rather than a single recipe, and outlines practical recommendations for when and how to apply KD effectively in NLP and broader deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Chang
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default, Task-Aware Engine for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a heuristic into a practical, multimodal toolkit that reliably shrinks large models into deployable students while preserving much of their utility. When treated as the central component of compression pipelines and matched to task and deployment constraints, KD delivers substantial gains in latency, memory, and communication efficiency. However, safe and effective use of KD requires careful, task-aware choices about what knowledge to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, how to handle data scarcity or privacy limits, and how to combine distillation with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, or student pretraining. This paper argues KD should be the default engine for model compression in deep learning and NLP, outlines its key mechanisms, highlights practical limitations and failure modes, and provides concrete recommendations for robust, deployed KD pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. KD operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, relational structure) and can be combined with complementary compression techniques and data strategies to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When tailored to model architecture, task demands, and available data, KD yields compact models that enable real-world deployment across modalities and domains.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic for transferring soft targets into a unifying toolkit that enables model compression, deployment on constrained devices, privacy-aware release, and modality transfer. By combining architectural mapping, contrastive and adversarial objectives, and data-free or federated setups, KD can preserve much of a teacher model's performance while drastically reducing footprint and computation. This makes KD essential for translating state-of-the-art large models into real-world, resource-limited, and privacy-sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Variants, and Practical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring aspects of the teacher’s predictive behavior and internal representations. A diverse set of methods—matching output distributions, aligning intermediate features, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher and data-free schemes, and task- or domain-aware adaptations—has been developed to address deployment constraints such as latency, memory, data availability, privacy, and multimodal inputs. Empirical work shows that when the distillation recipe is matched to model architectures, data conditions, and deployment constraints, students can retain much of the teacher’s performance while offering practical efficiency gains; however, trade-offs and open challenges remain around robustness, domain shift, and faithful transfer of rare or fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Conditional Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and mature training paradigm that enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often preserving—sometimes improving—task performance. As a practical tool, KD spans logits matching, intermediate-representation alignment, multi-teacher ensembles, data-free and zero-shot schemes, and combinations with pruning, quantization, or architecture-aware design. Its success in deployment hinges on matching distillation recipes to data availability, model capacity, and application constraints; when so matched, KD enables deployable students that recover much of teacher behavior, but predictable failure modes (capacity mismatch, domain shift, teacher errors, privacy and fairness concerns) require complementary methods and careful protocol design.

papers_seen.author: Callahan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, widely applicable strategy for compressing large neural networks into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation enables deployment of powerful pretrained models in resource-constrained settings, supports specialization (e.g., task or domain adaptation), and can be combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, pruning, architecture search) to produce practical, production-ready models. Advances in distillation methodology — including multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, teacher meta-learning, and task-aware layer-wise alignment — address fundamental challenges of capacity mismatch, information selection, and optimization stability, leading to more robust and efficient student models. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of any production-focused compression pipeline for deep learning and NLP systems, and that research emphasis on better teacher–student dynamics and task-aware transfer will yield the largest practical gains.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, Practical Benefits and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a simple teacher–student logit-matching trick into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large models and adapting their knowledge to resource- and data-constrained settings. Effective distillation operates at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational signals), interacts strongly with data and augmentation choices, and is most useful when combined with complementary compression methods and careful teacher–student design. While KD often yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance, its success depends on dealing with data availability, domain shift, teacher quality, and optimization dynamics—areas that remain active research directions.

papers_seen.author: Rosales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When carefully designed to match student capacity, task requirements, and available data, distillation reliably reduces inference cost and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. Its practical success depends on selecting appropriate distilled signals (logits, features, relations), combining KD with complementary compression primitives (pruning, architecture search, quantization), and addressing open problems such as data scarcity, teacher error transfer, and robustness across distributions.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Short
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable technique for producing smaller, faster models from large pretrained teachers. KD operates through multiple signals (soft outputs, intermediate representations, relational structure) and yields substantial efficiency gains when paired with complementary methods and task-aware design. However, KD alone cannot guarantee robustness, fairness, or optimal hardware utilization: achieving production-grade compression requires matching distillation objectives to data availability, architecture mismatch, privacy constraints, and combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture adaptation. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the core of a multi-tool compression pipeline—central to practical deployment but reliant on deliberate system-level choices to realize its benefits reliably.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Effective Practices and Practical Recommendations for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression are practical, versatile tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across computer vision, multimodal, and natural language processing tasks, distillation can preserve or approximate teacher performance while substantially reducing model size and latency. Successful distillation strategies go beyond matching final logits: they exploit intermediate representations, task-aware selection of teacher signals, many-to-many layer mappings, and feature-level or adversarial training to transfer richer knowledge. Combining these approaches yields compact models that retain robustness and task performance, and that can be further complemented by pruning or hardware-aware compression for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Stein
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Work has expanded beyond the original teacher→student soft-label matching to include intermediate-representation imitation, multi-teacher and adaptive-teacher schedules, self- and teacher-free variants, and data-aware protocols (including data-free and privacy-preserving approaches). Empirical and theoretical analyses show KD can preserve much of teacher performance while substantially lowering latency, memory, and sometimes communication cost; success depends on matching distillation signals to student capacity, handling data heterogeneity, and combining KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Remaining challenges include robustness to domain shift and adversaries, preserving rare-token or long-tail behaviors, automating signal and teacher selection, and reliable operation without original training data.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Conditional
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. KD operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate features, relational signals) and is most effective when integrated with complementary practices such as pre-training, architecture-aware design, data-side strategies, and other compression techniques. However, its success is conditional on deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or mismatched data, and how to mitigate propagation of teacher errors or biases. Treating KD as a flexible toolkit rather than a single recipe yields the best results for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Current Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and graph domains, KD has been adapted into many variants — matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, progressive module replacement, online/multi-teacher training, and data-free or privacy-aware pipelines — often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation targets, student preparation, and data strategies are chosen carefully. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness is limited by teacher quality, data availability or privacy, teacher–student architectural mismatch, and risks of transferring undesirable teacher behaviors. Practical deployment benefits from combining KD with complementary compression and data strategies, designing student-aware teacher signals, and accounting for robustness and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and structural signals. A broad suite of distillation techniques—soft-target (logit) matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and channel-wise transfers, multi-stage or multi-teacher schemes, and data- or generator-based approaches—enables large reductions in parameter count and latency while retaining much of the teacher’s effectiveness. Distillation is most effective when combined with task-aware design (student-aware teacher choices, layer alignment or projectors, and data strategies) and complementary compression primitives (architecture search, pruning, quantization). Important limitations include capacity mismatch, optimization instability, propagation of teacher errors or low-frequency behavior loss, and constraints from limited or private data; addressing these requires careful choice of signals, student architectures, and training curricula.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce computation, memory, and latency while retaining much of the original performance. A diverse set of techniques—matching soft outputs (logits), aligning intermediate representations, many-to-many layer mappings, attention- or relation-aware objectives, multi-teacher schedules, and data-free or privacy-conscious procedures—have been developed and evaluated across vision, speech, language, and domain-specific settings. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, the availability or synthesis of distillation data, and integration with complementary compression techniques; remaining challenges include domain shift, propagation of teacher errors, and principled teacher selection.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Not Sufficient Tool for Compression and Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling substantial runtime, memory, and latency gains while preserving much of predictive performance. KD is effective across modalities and deployment regimes, but its success depends on careful method choice, teacher quality, data availability, and combination with complementary compression strategies. Future progress requires deeper theoretical understanding, better automation for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive settings, and principled integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role and Evolving Practices of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a fundamental and versatile approach for model compression and knowledge transfer in deep learning and NLP. It enables compact, efficient student models that retain much of a teacher's performance, supports deployment on resource-constrained devices, and can be adapted to privacy-sensitive or distributed settings. Recent advances extend distillation beyond simple logits matching to many-to-many layer mapping, task-adaptive compression, teacher-aware training, adversarial and data-free scenarios, and robustness-aware objectives. Together these developments show that distillation is both a practical engineering tool and a rich research paradigm for addressing capacity, data availability, privacy, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Capabilities, Integrations, and Conditional Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible pathway to convert large, high-performing deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. KD operates at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate representations, relational structure) and can be combined with complementary compression techniques such as quantization, pruning, and architecture-aware surgery to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its empirical strengths include preserving much of teacher performance while enabling large efficiency gains; its limitations arise from teacher–student mismatch, data availability constraints, possible propagation of teacher defects, and robustness or fairness trade-offs. Effective deployment treats KD as the core of a hybrid compression toolkit and requires deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align layers and capacities, how to handle scarce or private data, and when to combine KD with low-precision numerics or structured pruning.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Methods, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring behavioral and representational signals from teachers. KD includes diverse techniques — soft-target supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer-mapping strategies, online and ensemble-to-single transfers, and selective sample or data-aware procedures — that are adapted to task, architecture, and deployment constraints. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and appropriate data strategies, KD can yield compact models that retain most teacher performance; however, success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, and data availability.

papers_seen.author: Salazar
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from teacher models. A broad toolkit has emerged—matching softened outputs, aligning feature or attention maps, adversarial and online schemes, data-centric interventions (augmentation, synthetic or data-free sampling), and architecture-aware methods (pruning, quantization, or student-aware design). Practical deployment requires selecting the right signals to transfer, addressing data limitations and domain shift, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques. While distilled models often recover much of a teacher's accuracy with substantial efficiency gains, open problems remain in robustness, fairness, privacy, and principled teacher–student alignment.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.
